question: What is the receptor classification of buprenorphine, and what clinically important property results from its partial agonist activity at the µ-opioid receptor?

answers.text: Partial µ-agonist and κ-antagonist — produces a ceiling effect on respiratory depression, and can precipitate withdrawal if given to a patient on full µ-agonists

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. Buprenorphine's partial µ-agonism means it activates µ-receptors to a submaximal level — producing adequate analgesia but with a ceiling on respiratory depression (safer in overdose). Its very high receptor affinity means it displaces full agonists (morphine, heroin), potentially precipitating acute withdrawal in dependent patients.

answers.text: Full µ-agonist with long duration — same efficacy as morphine but with extended half-life

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Buprenorphine is NOT a full agonist. Full µ-agonists (morphine, fentanyl) have no ceiling on respiratory depression. Buprenorphine's partial agonism is what gives it the safety advantage (ceiling effect) that makes it suitable for outpatient opioid use disorder treatment.

answers.text: Pure opioid antagonist — blocks all opioid effects and is used only for overdose reversal

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: That describes naloxone or naltrexone (pure antagonists). Buprenorphine has intrinsic agonist activity (partial) — it reduces pain and suppresses withdrawal, unlike a pure antagonist which would precipitate withdrawal and provide no analgesia.

answers.text: Mixed κ-agonist and µ-antagonist — produces dysphoria and is not used clinically for analgesia

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: That profile (κ-agonist/µ-antagonist) describes older agents like pentazocine, which cause dysphoria. Buprenorphine is the opposite — partial µ-AGONIST (some euphoria/analgesia) plus κ-ANTAGONIST (may contribute to antidepressant effect).

overallFeedback.feedback: Understanding receptor classification (full agonist vs partial agonist vs antagonist) predicts clinical properties: ceiling effects, ability to precipitate withdrawal, and overdose safety profile.

Buprenorphine's partial µ-agonism gives it a unique clinical niche: ceiling on respiratory depression (safety), high receptor affinity (displaces full agonists), and adequate efficacy for moderate pain and opioid substitution therapy.
